svg.title: Motor neuron: longitudinal section, with a magnified transverse section of the myelinated axon
svg.desc: A multipolar motor neuron. Branched dendrites and the cell body with its nucleus are on the left. The axon leaves the cell body at the axon hillock and runs to the right as one continuous fibre, covered by myelin sheaths formed by Schwann cells, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier. Near the end it branches into axon terminals ending in synaptic knobs. A magnified transverse section shows the axon surrounded by spiral layers of myelin and the Schwann cell cytoplasm and nucleus.

g.data-info: Short, branched extensions of the cell body. They receive signals from other neurons at synapses and carry impulses towards the cell body.

Contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm and organelles (e.g. ribosomes, mitochondria). It makes proteins such as neurotransmitter enzymes and integrates incoming signals. In a motor neuron it lies in the spinal cord or brainstem.
Cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body. Signals are summed here; if the membrane reaches threshold, an action potential begins at the hillock and initial segment.

A single long fibre that carries action potentials away from the cell body to the axon terminals. Motor axons can be up to about 1 m long. The axoplasm is continuous from the hillock to the terminals.
The axon divides near its target into terminal branches, which lose their myelin. Each carries the impulse to a synaptic knob.

Swollen ends of the terminal branches (terminal boutons). They contain mitochondria and vesicles of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, released by exocytosis at the neuromuscular junction onto a muscle fibre.
Holds the DNA that codes for the neuron’s proteins. In motor neurons it is large, round and central, with a prominent nucleolus.
Region of the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosomes are assembled; prominent because neurons synthesise a lot of protein.
Many layers of Schwann cell membrane wrapped round the axon. Rich in lipid, it insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane between nodes, making conduction faster.

A glial cell of the peripheral nervous system. Each Schwann cell wraps its membrane round one section of axon (one internode) to form myelin; its nucleus and most of its cytoplasm lie outside the myelin.

A short gap (about 1 µm) between neighbouring Schwann cells where the axon membrane is exposed. Voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels are clustered here, so the action potential jumps from node to node: saltatory conduction.

svg.text: Not to scale. The axon (up to about 1 m long) and the internodes
(about 100 × the fibre diameter) are shortened, shown by the break.

g.data-info: Thin layer of Schwann cell cytoplasm outside the myelin.
The flattened nucleus of the Schwann cell, pushed to the outside of the myelin sheath.
Concentric layers of Schwann cell plasma membrane, formed as the Schwann cell wraps round the axon in a spiral; the cytoplasm is squeezed out from between the layers.
Cytoplasm of the axon, enclosed by the axon membrane, which carries the action potential.
Plasma membrane of the axon. Under the myelin it has few ion channels; channels are concentrated at the nodes.

svg.text: Myelin = layers of Schwann cell membrane wrapped in a spiral round the axon.
